facts: The Saint-Émilion classification dates from 1955, covers wines of the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation, and is updated every 10 years or so.
The classification has three levels: Premier grand cru classé A, Premier grand cru classé B, and Grand cru classé.
As of the 2022 classification, Château Figeac and Château Pavie are the two estates at the highest level.
Wines are typically blended, and the three main grapes are Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon.
The appellation sits on the right bank of the Dordogne in Bordeaux's Libourne subregion and covers 13,000 acres.
Sancerre is an AOC in the eastern Loire, best known for white wine from Sauvignon blanc, with red and rosé made from Pinot noir.
White Sancerre was one of the original AOCs awarded in 1936, and the same area was designated for red wines in 1959.
Sauternes is a sweet white wine made from Sémillon, Sauvignon blanc and Muscadelle grapes affected by Botrytis cinerea, also called noble rot.
Autumn mist forms where the cooler Ciron meets the warmer Garonne, and it promotes noble rot before the midday sun dries the grapes.
Sweet wine harvests involve hand-picking only the ripest berries, and production varies widely from vintage to vintage.
The 1855 classification has two levels, Premiers Crus and Deuxièmes Crus, with Château d'Yquem alone ranked Premier Cru Supérieur.
Five communes may use the name Sauternes: Barsac, Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac, and Barsac may also use its own appellation.
Vosne-Romanée AOC is only for red wine with Pinot noir as the main grape, and it covers the communes of Vosne-Romanée and Flagey-Échezeaux.
There are six Grand Cru vineyards in Vosne-Romanée and two in Flagey-Échezeaux, plus 15 Premier Cru vineyards across the two communes.
The Grand Crus in Vosne-Romanée are La Tâche, La Grande Rue, La Romanée, Romanée-Conti, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and Richebourg.
Flagey-Échezeaux has two Grand Crus, Echézeaux and Grands Échezeaux.
Romanée-Conti and La Tâche are monopoles of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti.
The AOC allows up to 15% total Chardonnay, Pinot blanc and Pinot gris in the red wines, though this is not practiced much.
Vouvray is a Loire Valley AOC in Touraine, just east of Tours, and is dedicated almost exclusively to Chenin blanc.
Cooler years favor dry (sec) and sparkling Vouvray, while warmer vintages favor sweet moelleux or liquoreux wines made by noble rot.
Labels may use Sec (under 4 g/L residual sugar), Demi-Sec (4 to 12 g/L), Moelleux (12 to 45 g/L) and Doux (over 45 g/L).
Vineyards sit on a plateau of gravel and clay over tuffeau, and cellars were dug into the tuffeau rock.
Sparkling Vouvray is made by the traditional method and can be pétillant (semi-sparkling) or mousseux (fully sparkling).
Germany has 13 quality wine regions (Anbaugebiete), and white wine is almost two thirds of production.
Prädikatswein levels are Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein, and they are linked to minimum potential alcohol.
Chaptalization is allowed only up to the QbA level, not for Prädikatswein, and Süssreserve may be added after fermentation.
Riesling is the benchmark grape and the most planted since the mid-1990s, and Spätburgunder (Pinot noir) leads among reds.
Mosel covers the valleys of the Mosel, Saar and Ruwer rivers, and before 1 August 2007 it was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer.
Riesling is the main grape, covering 59.7% of vineyard area in 2008, and white varieties cover 91% of the total.
Steep slopes and slate soils shape the wines, and many of the best vineyards have no topsoil at all, just broken slate.
The northerly climate gives light Rieslings that tend to be lower in alcohol, crisp and high in acidity, with flowery aromas.
The region has six districts (Bereiche), 19 Großlagen and 524 Einzellagen.
The Calmont vineyard in Bremm, at a 65° incline, is the steepest recorded vineyard in the world.
Pfalz had 58,560 acres under cultivation in 2022, making it the second largest German wine region after Rheinhessen.
It is one of the warmest, sunniest and driest German wine regions, lying in the lee of the Haardt Mountains.
The region has two districts, Südliche Weinstraße in the south and Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstraße in the north.
Production is split 61% white and 39% red, and the wines are traditionally dry (trocken) and full bodied.
Riesling has always had a strong foothold in the Mittelhaardt, and Spätburgunder, Portugieser and Dornfelder plantings have grown.
Rheingau makes up only 3 percent of the German vineyard area but has been the source of many historically important innovations in German winemaking.
Most vineyards are on south-facing slopes below the Taunus mountains, which gives excellent growing conditions in a northerly latitude.
The region spans about 31 miles from end to end.
Spätlese was first made at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775, and Auslese followed in 1787, laying the ground for the Prädikat system.
Assyrtiko is the flagship grape, a high acid variety that gives full-bodied wines averaging 13.5% abv.
Vines are trained in a basket system called kouloura and woven into rings, with the grapes inside, to protect them from wind and sun.
Santorini is immune to phylloxera because its volcanic soils contain very little clay, so many vines have centuries old roots.
The vineyard soils are very poor, made of volcanic ash and rocks, and the area has strong winds and low rainfall.
Santorini wine must be at least 75% Assyrtiko, with the rest Athiri and/or Aidani, and it is bone-dry and high in acid.
Vinsanto must be at least 51% Assyrtiko, made from sun-dried grapes (12 to 14 days), and aged at least 24 months in oak.
Tokaj is known for Tokaji aszú, the world's oldest botrytized wine, and it was declared a World Heritage Site in 2002.
Furmint and Hárslevelű are the main varieties, and only Yellow Muscat, Kabar, Kövérszőlő and Zéta are also officially permitted.
The terroir is clay or loess soil on volcanic subsoil, with sunny south-facing slopes.
The Tisza and Bodrog rivers help create the conditions for noble rot and the drying of the grapes.
Cellars carved from solid rock between 1400 and 1600 AD stay at about 50 to 54°F and have 85 to 95% humidity.
A wine can be recognized as DOC only after its area has been IGT for at least five years.
DOCG applies only to wines that have been DOC for at least seven years, and bottles carry a control band.
DOCG wines undergo mandatory chemical-physical and organoleptic analysis, batch by batch, during bottling.
Amarone became a DOCG of its own, as did Recioto della Valpolicella, by ministerial decree of 24 March 2010.
It is made from partially dried grapes: Corvina and/or Corvinone (45 to 95%), Rondinella (5 to 30%) and other approved red grapes (up to 25%).
Drying is called appassimento, and it typically takes 120 days and ends around the end of January or beginning of February.
After fermentation, the wine must age at least 2 years, calculated from 1 January of the year following the harvest.
